metadata.title: Why don’t more boys want to become teachers? The effect of a gendered profession on students’ career expectations

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old students from 49 participating countries, with analytic subsets of 49 countries for descriptive/logistic analyses and 30 countries for the multilevel hierarchical Bernoulli logit (HGLM) models. To account for the clustered PISA design (students nested within schools) and to obtain unbiased standard errors, the authors compute descriptive statistics and binomial logistic regressions using balanced replication weights (BRR). For the multilevel models, they also report using senate weights to ensure each country contributes equally to the pooled analyses. Missing values are handled via chained equations (ICE) in Stata 15, and plausible values are incorporated in the HGLM models by running the models 10 times (once per plausible value) and combining estimates per PISA procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2015 student questionnaire data for 15-year-olds in 49 countries for descriptive and country-specific logistic regression analyses, and restricts to 30 countries for the pooled three-level hierarchical Bernoulli logit (HGLM) models. Countries are excluded from HGLM analyses when key country-level variables are missing: teacher salary relative to GDP per capita, gender egalitarianism, and the share of male teachers in lower-secondary education. Specifically excluded are Albania, Algeria, Argentina, China (Beijing/Shanghai/Jiangsu/Guangdong), Costa Rica, Georgia, Kosovo, Lebanon, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, Moldova, Russia, Trinidad and Tobago, and Vietnam due to missing average teacher salary data; and the United Arab Emirates, the Dominican Republic, Malta, Qatar, and Chinese Taipei due to missing shares of men and women in the teaching profession. At the student level, the dependent variable is binary and is coded from an open-ended occupation question; the analysis includes students expecting to work as a teacher (in general or by ISCO-08 teaching categories) versus not expecting a teaching career, and the authors also run robustness checks on the subsample of students expecting professional occupations.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical Bernoulli logit (odds ratios); no ML metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged gender, family SES, and country-level indicators (share of male teachers, gender egalitarianism beliefs, and teacher salary relative to GDP) to model whether students expected a teaching career, finding that boys are less likely than girls to expect teaching and that the gender gap is smaller where the share of male teachers is higher. This indicates that policies increasing male teacher representation and visibility may reduce gendered career expectations, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 student questionnaire data on 15-year-olds’ teaching career expectations, coded from an open-ended question about the job they expect to have around age 30. The dependent variable is binary (expect teaching career vs not) and is modeled using hierarchical Bernoulli logit models with students nested within schools and countries, incorporating PISA plausible values for math/reading/science controls by running models across 10 plausible values and combining estimates. The pooled HGLM analyses use BRR for standard errors in logistic regressions and senate weights to ensure equal country contribution in the multilevel models, with missing values handled via chained equations (ICE) in Stata. Results show boys are generally less likely than girls to aspire to teaching, and country contexts matter: higher shares of male teachers are associated with higher odds of expecting teaching (stronger for boys), while higher gender egalitarianism is associated with lower odds (also stronger for boys). The paper reports odds ratios and standard errors rather than predictive ML metrics, and the single-wave cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
